role: Server at a hotpot chain restaurant
headline: Out of middle school and up from Zhoukou in Henan with someone from the same village, sleeping in the staff dorm round the corner, a server minding six tables at a hotpot chain restaurant in Chaoyang, Beijing, who means to run a restaurant of their own one day
unit: A company-run branch of a national hotpot chain in Chaoyang district, Beijing (four hundred seats, open until two in the morning)
level: You can carry a pot and remember the menu, and you've got the hang of ordering on the tablet. Three tables on your own, no problem; six and you're scrambling, and when a customer loses their temper all you know to do is fetch the team leader
intro: You rode a slow green train all night to Beijing with an older girl from your village, and the next morning you were standing in this hotpot restaurant's morning meeting. The team leader handed you a uniform and an earpiece and said your mentor is the woman in Section Three; follow her first, and watch how she walks. As of today, in this four-hundred-seat restaurant, six tables are yours.
salary_note: Estimate: at a chain hotpot restaurant in Beijing, servers get base pay plus a piece rate, with meals and a dorm bed, and take home over twenty percent more than the national figure. Once you're a store manager you take a share of the restaurant's profit, which in Beijing runs well above the national figure for store managers.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Minding the tables and reading the room

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Scan-to-order, placing orders and taking payment

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 107 related job listings nationwide, 1 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Morning meeting at the restaurant. The store manager stands by the door, and everyone says one thing: which table was unhappy yesterday, and why. When it's your turn, you say Table Seven found the broth too weak, and the manager asks you to explain why you didn't top it up.

Opening: wipe the pot rings, test the induction hobs, fill the sauce bar, sesame paste, crushed garlic, coriander, scallions, a bowl of each. Each of your six tables gets four place settings, every pair of chopsticks pointing the same way.

Doors open. People are already waiting. You put on your earpiece, hear the team leader call "Section Three, party of two," and step forward: seat them, hand over aprons and phone pouches, ask how spicy they want the broth.

The rush. A delivery robot dings to a stop by your table and you set out tripe and duck intestine plate by plate; Table Five has a child, so you fetch a high chair and a little bowl and push the pot further in.

Staff lunch in the little room at the back: a tub of braised pork with potatoes, a tub of rice. Then back to the dorm behind the restaurant for a lie-down. Eight to a room in bunks; someone's gaming, someone's already asleep.

The evening rush. The waiting area is past number two hundred, the folding chairs at the door all taken. You carry a boiling split pot through the crowd, saying over and over, "Excuse me, careful, it's hot."
It's a birthday at Table Nine, and you and the rest of Section Three carry out the longevity noodles, clapping and singing. The birthday girl is about your age. She cries, and you nearly do too.
The last table leaves. Wipe down, clear the pots, mop, set out tomorrow's plates. Walking back to the dorm, the lights over Sanlitun are still on, and the soles of your feet feel like two bricks.

ladder.title: Server
ladder.focus: Greet, seat, take orders, bring the pots, top up broth, clear tables, several tables at a time. You make team leader on quick hands, remembering your customers and few complaints.

ladder.title: Team Leader
ladder.focus: Lead five or six servers in one section: assign tables, cover gaps, handle ordinary complaints, train new apprentices. You move up on your section's table turnover, its good reviews and the people you bring on.

ladder.title: Floor Manager
ladder.focus: Run the whole front of house: rotas, the waiting list, the rush, escalated complaints, the morning meeting. You move up on the store's rating, its complaint rate and the team leaders you turn out.

ladder.title: Store Manager
ladder.focus: Run one restaurant's people, money, stock and food safety: hiring, roles, costs, revenue, the store rating, with a share of the profit. You move up on the store's results and on training people who can open new branches.

ladder.title: Area Manager
ladder.focus: Run five or six restaurants in one area: visit them, coach their managers, open new ones, pick sites, answer to head office on targets. You hold the job on the area's results and its bench of store managers.

ai_tasks.name: Scan-to-order, placing orders and taking payment
ai_tasks.how: Customers scan the code on the table to order, add dishes and pay, and the order goes straight to the kitchen. Servers only deal with changes, returns, discounts, and old people who can't work their phones.

ai_tasks.name: Queue numbers, calling tables and reservations
ai_tasks.how: A mini-app hands out queue numbers, takes bookings and texts people when their turn comes, and can estimate how long the wait will be. A person only goes out at the rush to calm customers who've waited too long.

ai_tasks.name: Running dishes and pots
ai_tasks.how: Delivery robots can carry plates from the pass to the table. Setting the pot on the table, laying out the plates, warning people it's hot, passing a dish to an old person's hand, is still the server's job.

ai_tasks.name: Rotas and stock forecasts
ai_tasks.how: The system forecasts footfall from past years, the weather and bookings, and drafts a first rota and stock list. Whose family has something on, who's training a newcomer, whether to keep two extra people at the weekend, the store manager changes by hand.

ai_tasks.name: Minding the tables and reading the room
ai_tasks.how: Topping up broth, changing bone plates, spotting which table is arguing, which child is about to touch the pot, whose birthday it is today: it takes a person moving round the tables with their eyes open.

ai_tasks.name: Handling complaints and incidents on the spot
ai_tasks.how: Broth splashed on a customer, something in the food, a drunk causing trouble: someone has to apologize there and then, decide what to do and take responsibility. At most AI helps write it down.

events.e_spill: Carrying a pot, your foot slipped and broth splashed a customer's trouser leg. You apologized in a panic; your mentor came over, took the pot, brought a plate of fruit and a clean towel, and the customer still left a good review.
events.e_feet: Over twenty thousand steps a shift, and in the first month you wore two blood blisters into the soles of your feet. Your mentor gave you a pair of her old soft-soled shoes, and said new shoes take three months to fit.
events.e_regular: A regular who comes every week learned your name and asks for your section every time. He says you remember he doesn't eat coriander better than his wife does.
events.e_new_year: The restaurant doesn't close for Spring Festival, and every seat for New Year's Eve was booked a month ahead. For the first time you didn't go home to Zhoukou for the New Year. After closing you video-called home from the dorm, and your mother held up the dumplings to show you.
events.e_drunk: A table that had drunk too much smashed a glass and pointed at you, cursing. You stood still; the team leader came over and put herself between you and them. That night you sat a long time on the back steps.
events.e_robot: The restaurant got three delivery robots, dinging their way from the pass to the tables. You walk half as far, but customers take dishes off the robot themselves, a plate of shrimp paste ended up on the floor, and in the end it was you who cleaned it up.
events.e_love: Every time you went to the pass, the young guy who preps in the kitchen handed your order out first. One night after closing he was waiting at the door, saying the grilled cold-noodle stall near the dorm was still open.
events.e_child_choke: A child at the next table choked on a meatball. You rushed over, put your arms around him from behind the way they taught you in training, and thrust upward, and the meatball came out. The mother held the child and cried, and your hands shook all night.
events.e_star: Your tables got the most good reviews this month, and you were named service star of your section: your photo went up on the wall of the staff corridor, with a ¥500 bonus. You transferred ¥400 of it to your mother.
events.e_scan: The restaurant switched entirely to scan-to-order: customers order and pay themselves. You no longer stand with a tablet taking down dish after dish, and the time it freed up went on minding two more tables.
events.e_slow: One year business was strangely slow, and by eight at night no one was queuing. The restaurant cut the piece rate; you took home over a thousand yuan less a month, and three people moved out of the dorm.
events.e_wedding: You got married, with the banquet back home in Zhoukou. Your mentor, the team leader and a few of your apprentices chipped in for a red envelope, and on video they shouted "Happy wedding!" together outside the restaurant.
events.e_inspect: Head office's mystery diners came, and none of you knew which table they were. When the month's rating report came down, your section lost a point: a customer waited three minutes for a broth top-up.
events.e_apprentice: Your first apprentice was a girl just turned eighteen, whose hands shook carrying a pot on day one. You said nothing, carried empty pots with her all afternoon, and the next day she carried a real one.
events.e_child: Your child was born. You only took a few days off, and at one year old the baby went back to Zhoukou for your mother to raise. Every night after closing you video-call from outside the dorm, and he's already asleep.
events.e_dashboard: Every morning the restaurant's system pushes out a dashboard: yesterday's table turnover, complaints, people who gave up waiting, good reviews by section. You no longer run the morning meeting on a hunch; you point at the dashboard and say which section slipped yesterday.
events.e_food_safety: A customer posted online that he'd found a hair in his food, and it was shared over a thousand times. You and your team went through the kitchen, the cold room and the security footage, section by section, and the next day you went to his home to apologize.
events.e_rent: You moved out of the staff dorm and rented a two-bedroom flat with your spouse in Yanjiao, out past the city line, and every day you ride the commuter bus into town. Half the bus is asleep; you're looking at the restaurant's dashboard.
events.e_knee: After more than ten years on your feet in the restaurant, your knees have started to hurt, and you hold the rail going downstairs. The doctor says it's strain and tells you to stand less, and you smile.
events.e_old_regular: The regular who remembered your name has gone completely white, and comes in with his grandson. Seeing you, he tells the boy: I watched this one grow up.
events.e_hometown: Your father went into hospital in Zhoukou and you took half a month off to go back. In the hospital corridor you watched the restaurant's live dashboard on your phone and called the person on duty several times.
events.e_young_staff: Fewer and fewer young people apply to wait tables, and the first thing they ask is whether they can avoid night shifts. The restaurant's robots went from three to six, and there are half as many people on the floor as when you started.

c_rider.title: Wanting to leave in the third month
c_rider.situation: The friend from your village who came out with you quit to deliver takeout, saying you can make eight or nine thousand a month, no need to put up with anyone's moods, and go out whenever you like. The soles of your feet still haven't healed, and your mentor says hang on three more months and they will.

options.label: Stay with your mentor
options.result: You hung on three more months. Your soles grew calluses, and you could carry a pot across six tables while remembering which one needed broth.

options.label: Go deliver takeout with your friend
options.result: You bought a second-hand e-bike, did thirty deliveries on your first day, and got lost twice inside housing compounds.
options.end: You became a takeout rider in Beijing, knowing the back gate of every compound in Chaoyang; passing that hotpot restaurant, you still glance in to see who's minding Section Three.

c_lead.title: Team Leader or not
c_lead.situation: The leader of Section Three has been moved to a new branch, and the store manager will pick someone from the section. You came later than the others but have the most good reviews; the other contender has been here a year longer and gets on well with the manager. A team leader trains newcomers and takes the complaints; less piece rate, a little more base pay.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: Every night after closing you stayed an extra half hour, writing down the regulars of every table in the section in a notebook. The store manager looked at your notebook and gave you a month's trial.

options.label: Mind tables for another two years
options.result: You kept your six tables, earned more on the piece rate and got off earlier. The other one became team leader, and complaints still often got passed over to you.

c_system.title: Learn the restaurant system's back end or not
c_system.situation: Head office has rolled out a new restaurant system: rotas, stock, complaints and the dashboard all in one. The store manager wants a young person to learn it first and then teach everyone. Learning it eats your afternoon break, and knowing it doesn't pay any more.

options.label: Learn it
options.result: You skipped your afternoon naps and went through the menus on the tablet one by one. A month later, whenever someone's shift was set wrong or too much of a dish was stocked, everyone came to ask you.

options.label: Let someone else learn it
options.result: You still went back to the dorm for a lie-down in the afternoons. Once the system went live, you asked about whatever you needed as you went, and that was enough.

c_new_store.title: Go with your mentor to open a branch in Zhengzhou
c_new_store.situation: Your mentor is going to open a new branch in Zhengzhou and asks if you'll come. Everything at a new branch, hiring, training, opening, starts from scratch; the pay is a bit lower than in Beijing, but it's close to Zhoukou, and you could go home at weekends.

options.label: Go with your mentor
options.result: At the new branch in Zhengzhou you hired twenty servers from nothing and taught them to carry pots and mind tables. On opening day the queue passed two hundred, and at weekends you take the hour-and-a-half high-speed train home.

options.label: Stay in Beijing
options.result: You saw your mentor off at the station. Before she left she gave you Section Three's notebook of regulars.

c_hall.title: Apply for Floor Manager
c_hall.situation: The restaurant's floor manager is moving up to run another branch, and the job means an exam: a written test on procedures, a role-play handling a complaint, and a talk on how you'd staff the rush. You've applied, and so has the section leader next door.

options.label: Apply
options.result: You wrote down every complaint you'd dealt with over the years. In the role-play the examiner played a furious customer; you stood and heard him out, apologized first, then asked how he'd like it put right.

options.label: Don't apply
options.result: The leader from next door got it. You still lead your section, and you get home on time after your shift.

c_hometown.title: Go back to Zhoukou and open a hotpot restaurant
c_hometown.situation: Your brother has found a shopfront in the county town in Zhoukou and wants to go in with you on a hotpot place; after all these years learning in Beijing, he says, you'd go back as the boss. But people in the county town will only spend a few dozen yuan on a meal.

options.label: Go back and open it
options.result: You set the tables and trained the servers the way your Beijing restaurant did, and brought longevity noodles to customers on their birthdays. The first year lost money; by the second, everyone in the county town with a birthday came to you.
options.end: You went back to Zhoukou and opened a hotpot restaurant in the county town, twenty tables; the servers you trained all say "excuse me, careful, it's hot" when they carry a pot.

options.label: Stay in Beijing
options.result: You sent your brother fifty thousand yuan and said you wouldn't come back just yet. After the call, you went back into the restaurant to run the briefing before evening service.

c_manager.title: Sit the Store Manager assessment
c_manager.situation: The company is promoting a batch of store managers, and the assessment looks at three things: the people you've trained, the rating of the floor you run, and a business plan you write for a restaurant. Pass, and you run one restaurant's people, money and stock; miss the revenue target, and you go back down.

options.label: Sit it
options.result: You wrote the plan until three in the morning, working through years of complaints, turnover and wastage. At the panel, the area manager asked what matters most in a restaurant, and you said whether people want to stay.

options.label: Wait a while
options.result: You said you weren't ready yet. That year you brought on two more team leaders, and one of them later made store manager before you.

c_kid_school.title: Where your child goes to school
c_kid_school.situation: Your child is about to start primary school. He could go in Beijing, but it means a stack of paperwork and no one to do the school run; in Zhoukou your mother would look after him, but you'd see him only a few times a year. As it happens, the company has an opening to transfer to a restaurant back in Henan.

options.label: Bring him to school in Beijing
options.result: You gathered a stack of paperwork, made trip after trip, and got him into school in Beijing. You and your spouse take turns asking for time off to collect him, and after school he does his homework in the restaurant's staff room.

options.label: Transfer to a restaurant in Henan
options.result: You transferred to a branch in Zhengzhou on noticeably less pay. Every weekend you drive back to Zhoukou, and your child waits for you at the door.

options.label: Leave him in Zhoukou
options.result: He stayed in Zhoukou. You video-call every night after closing, and bit by bit he stops wanting to answer.

c_region.title: Take on an area
c_region.situation: The company wants you as area manager for six restaurants on the west side of Beijing. You'd be on the road every day visiting them, holding meetings, coaching people, and your own restaurant would go to an apprentice you trained. Two of those six have been at the bottom of the rankings for a long time.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every day you drive round three restaurants, sit by the kitchen door watching dishes go out, sit in the waiting area watching customers' faces. Six months on, one of the two at the bottom has climbed up.

options.label: Keep this restaurant
options.result: You recommended someone else. You still stand at the door every morning running the meeting, hearing everyone say which table was unhappy yesterday.

endings.retire: On your last day you still arrived at half past nine and stood at the door hearing everyone say which table was unhappy yesterday. The last to speak was a new girl, who said Table Seven found the broth too weak, and you asked her why she hadn't topped it up. After closing you walked once round the six tables of Section Three and straightened a pair of chopsticks.
endings.burnout: That winter your knees and back gave out together, and you had to lean on the wall to stand through a morning meeting. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You handed in your notice and went back to Zhoukou. A new hotpot place opened in the county town, and you ate there once; watching the server carry a pot, you couldn't help saying, careful, it's hot.

stages: You mind the six tables of Section Three: greet and seat, hand out aprons and phone pouches, ask about the broth, order on the tablet, set out each plate as it arrives, top up the broth when it's low, change bone plates when they're full. Your mentor is in the next section, and when you don't know what to do you glance at her; she points with her chin, and you know what to fetch.

Section Three's five or six servers are yours to lead. Before service you assign tables: who takes the windows, who takes the private rooms. At the rush you circle the section, cover any table that's short, and step in first when a customer flares up. New apprentices follow you, and you teach them to walk close to the wall and to call out before carrying a pot. You carry fewer pots now, and watch more people.

The whole front of house is yours: you run the morning meeting, you draw up the rota, and when the waiting list passes two hundred you go out with snacks to calm people who are tired of waiting. Every complaint a team leader can't handle comes to you, and as you apologize you're working out how to make sure the customer doesn't leave angry. Every night you go through the system's good reviews and complaints.

A restaurant is yours now: four hundred seats, over eighty staff, each month's revenue and cost sheets. Every day you look at the dashboard first, then at the kitchen's cold room and the dishes going out; hiring, roles, who gets made team leader, all need your nod. When head office's rating team or market regulators come, you walk them round; at night, after the last table has gone, you still take a turn through the front of house.

You run six restaurants in one area. Every day you drive to two or three, sitting in the waiting area watching customers' faces, standing at the pass watching the food; once a week you meet head office about revenue, complaints and staff turnover. Which restaurant needs a new manager, which mall a new branch goes into: you write the proposal, you do the negotiating. Three of the managers you trained have already opened new branches in other cities.
work: An old woman can't make sense of the QR code on the table. You crouch beside her, read the dishes aloud one by one, order for her on the tablet, and switch the meat to half portions.

A couple at one of your tables starts arguing, and the girl cries. You don't go over to intervene; you just quietly swap in a fresh pack of tissues and add a ladle of broth to the pot so it won't boil dry.

At closing you notice one heat setting on Table Five's induction hob isn't working. You write down exactly which hob and which setting in the handover book, and the next day the repairman goes straight to it.
Friday evening rush, and someone in the section is off sick. You reshuffle your six tables and his five, take three extra yourself, and your section gets not a single complaint that night.

Your apprentice's first time minding tables alone, he orders the wrong broth for a table. You don't say anything in front of the customers; you swap the broth in the kitchen, come back with a complimentary snack, and after closing you go through the order with him.
A foreign customer can't pick up shrimp paste with chopsticks. You fetch a small spoon and a slotted ladle and mime how to scoop it out of the pot; he gets it and gives you a thumbs-up.

On National Day the waiting list hits three hundred. You have a table set up in the waiting area with fruit and snacks, and phone everyone who's waited over an hour one by one to ask if they'd like to rebook.

A customer says there's a tiny insect in his broth and demands to see whoever's in charge. You carry the pot to the kitchen and check the ingredients in front of him, waive the bill, and then stand talking with him at the door for ten minutes.

Drawing up next month's May Day rota, you print the system's first draft and go through it name by name: whose child is little, who's already worked ten days straight this month, who's taking a driving test.

At the month-end accounts, beef wastage is ten percent higher than last month. You and the kitchen supervisor go through the dish records and the cold room logs sheet by sheet, and find one batch was sliced too thick and over-portioned.

Interviewing a floor manager who's jumping ship from another hotpot chain, you don't ask how many people he's managed; you just have him stand on the floor through an evening rush. Before he leaves, he helps up a child who's fallen, and you tell him to start the next day.

Head office wants your restaurant to push a new broth. You look at the cost card and say it won't sell at that price in this neighborhood. You put the prices at three nearby restaurants and your own average spend per head into a table and send it to the area manager.

One restaurant at the bottom of the rankings has had the most complaints three months running. You spend a week sitting in it, and in the end replace the store manager with someone you trained back in Section Three.

Viewing units in a new mall, the leasing manager shows you the best one. You sit in the mall from morning till night counting how many people pass the door in each hour, and in the end choose the unit next to the cinema.

At the area's managers' meeting, one manager says there are too many complaints about robots delivering to the wrong table. You have him pull a week of complaints, find they're all on the same aisle where the corner is too tight, and changing the route cuts them by more than half.
past: You grew up in the countryside outside Zhoukou with your grandmother while your parents worked far away. Weddings and funerals in the village meant banquets set out in the courtyard, and from a small child you helped carry the dishes, fast and steady.
You didn't get into high school after the entrance exam, and spent six months working in a restaurant in the county town, washing dishes and carrying plates for ¥1,500 a month.

You went to the county vocational school for a year of car mechanics, decided you weren't cut out for it and dropped out. You stayed at home; your grandmother said nothing, just cooked you a bowl of noodles every day.

A girl from the village a few years older than you came home for New Year and posed for photos in her hotpot restaurant uniform. The Beijing restaurants give you meals and a bed, she said, you can make five or six thousand a month, and if you're good you can become a store manager.
You went with her to a branch in Zhengzhou for a three-month trial. You burned your hands twice carrying pots, but you loved the bustle. If you want to get on, she said, go to Beijing.

You got your health certificate, packed a woven nylon bag, and boarded the slow green train to Beijing with her. At the edge of the village your grandmother pressed a bag of boiled eggs into your hands.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Beijing's urban employee pension scheme. The restaurant paid in on the minimum base for the first few years, and moving cities meant transferring your record, so in retirement you get about 40% of your last monthly salary; back in your hometown, counted by the years transferred there, it would be somewhat less.
scenes: Your first week of retirement you still wake after nine, wondering what to say at today's morning meeting, and only once you've worked it out do you remember you don't have to go.

The company asks you back to teach new store managers once a month. You don't talk about procedures; you talk about customers you've met, and when you get to the child who choked on a meatball, the room goes quiet.
You take your grandson for hotpot. The server brings the pot and says, "Excuse me, careful, it's hot," and your grandson says it after him. You laugh, and give the server a good review.
For the first few months back in Zhoukou you couldn't sit still at home. Every evening you walked round the county town, looking to see whether anyone was queuing outside the restaurants.

A new hotpot place in the county town asks you to train its servers two afternoons a week. You teach them to carry a pot, to walk, to remember what customers like, the way your mentor once taught you.

An old colleague in Beijing sends a photo: the Section Three you used to mind has become little self-order tables with a robot standing by them. He says there are only a dozen or so people on the floor now.
For the first month after leaving the hotpot restaurant, whenever you hear a ding, you glance toward the door without thinking.
The apprentice you trained at the restaurant has become a store manager, and posts a photo of the morning meeting captioned: my mentor taught me, start with which table was unhappy yesterday.

You went back to that hotpot restaurant once more. The waiting area at the door is an electronic screen now, and a robot shows you to your seat. You sit a while, waiting for a real person to ask how spicy you want the broth.

Lots of hotpot restaurants have handed ordering, queue numbers and running dishes to machines. But whose child is about to touch the pot, which table is in a bad mood today, still needs someone standing by the tables watching.

Your knees ache whenever the weather turns grey, worn that way by twenty thousand steps a day in the restaurant. When the family has hotpot at New Year, you still get up out of habit and top up everyone's broth.
The regular who remembered your name has passed on. His grandson comes in to eat and says his grandpa always told people there was a server in Beijing who remembered he didn't eat coriander.

closing.retire: One evening many years later, the family sits round the hotpot. You get up for the slotted ladle and, on the way, turn every pair of chopsticks on the table to point the same way. Your granddaughter asks why. So a customer can pick them up the moment they reach out, you say.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you sit in the courtyard of your old home in Zhoukou. Someone in the village is holding a banquet, and young people carry dishes past you. You call out, "Keep to the edge," and they turn and smile at you.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find the notebook of regulars' tastes, its paper gone yellow. The first page says: Table Seven, no coriander, broth a little saltier. You look at it a long time, then put it back in the drawer.
